metadata.methods_description: Participants performed a virtual-town courier task followed by free recall of delivered items. Read-only sessions generated training data for classifiers. In closed-loop sessions, classifiers predicted recall success and stimulus presentation was timed to coincide with predicted good or poor memory encoding.

citation_details.title: Causal and Chronological Relationships Predict Memory Organization for Nonlinear Narratives
citation_details.author: James W. Antony, Angelo Lozano, Pahul Dhoat, Janice Chen, Kelly A. Bennion
citation_details.abstract: While recounting an experience, one can employ multiple strategies to transition from one part to the next. For instance, if the event was learned out of linear order, one can recall events according to the time they were learned (temporal), similar events (semantic), events occurring nearby in time (chronological), or events produced by the current event (causal). To disentangle the importance of these factors, we had participants watch the nonlinear narrative, Memento, under different task instructions and presentation orders. For each scene of the film, we also separately computed semantic and causal networks. We then contrasted the evidence for temporal, semantic, chronological, or causal strategies during recall. Critically, there was stronger evidence for the causal and chronological strategies than semantic or temporal strategies. citation_details.title: Decoding EEG for optimizing naturalistic memory
citation_details.author: Joseph H. Rudoler, James P Bruska, Woohyeuk Chang, Matthew R. Dougherty, Brandon S Katerman, David J. Halpern, Nicholas B. Diamond, Michael J. Kahana
citation_details.abstract: Background Spectral features of human electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings during learning predict subsequent recall variability. New method Capitalizing on these fluctuating neural features, we develop a non-invasive closed-loop (NICL) system for real-time optimization of human learning. Participants play a virtual navigation and memory game; recording multi-session data across days allowed us to build participant-specific classification models of recall success. In subsequent closed-loop sessions, our platform manipulated the timing of memory encoding, selectively presenting items during periods of predicted good or poor memory function based on EEG features decoded in real time. Results We observed greater memory modulation (difference between recall rates when presenting items during predicted good vs. poor learning periods) for participants with higher out-of-sample classification accuracy. citation_details.title: LaBraM at Scale: Scaling Data and Models for EEG Pretraining
citation_details.author: Junyu Pan, Ruicheng Yin, Bao‐Liang Lu, Dongsheng Li, Wei-Long Zheng, Yansen Wang
citation_details.abstract: LaBraM, an early EEG foundation model, demonstrated that large-scale EEG pretraining can yield strong representations for diverse downstream tasks. Building on this foundation, we expand pretraining data and model capacity while retaining its core encoder and objective. We train ten encoders with 5.8 million to 1.97 billion parameters on three EEG collections spanning 25,067 to 79,910 hours, adapting signal preparation and training to heterogeneous recordings. Across 23 tasks, Atom-L* reaches 59.05% mean balanced accuracy at its best evaluated full fine-tuning (Full-FT) checkpoint, 3.61 percentage points above the strongest baseline EEG foundation model. Quark-G leads linear probing (LP) at 54.33%, a 1.24-point margin. Both also lead average task rank. At the last evaluated checkpoints, larger encoders improve Full-FT more consistently than LP, and stronger LP does not guarantee stronger Full-FT. citation_details.title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment
citation_details.author: Ryota Kanai
citation_details.abstract: Studies of data scaling in electroencephalography (EEG) and related noninvasive recordings suggest that simple wearable devices could eventually reveal more about cognitive states. However, publicly available EEG data are difficult to combine. Different laboratories record different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised learning can exploit such data, but representations learned only with EEG signals have not consistently produced feature representations that are directly effective for decoding the cognitive state. We therefore aimed to incorporate task information by embedding experimental instructions, stimuli and response demands in a common semantic space, and trained an EEG encoder to align signals from a single anterior--posterior differential channel with those task vectors. citation_details.title: Spectral Correlates of Encoding Distinguish Good from Poor Learners
citation_details.author: Benjamin E Falkenburg, Adam W. Broitman, Michael J. Kahana
citation_details.abstract: Individuals vary in their ability to encode and recall new experiences, yet neural markers of memory have rarely been linked to these trait-level differences. Subsequent memory effects (SMEs) identify patterns of neural activity during encoding that predict whether an item will later be remembered or forgotten. In scalp EEG, SMEs are typically characterized by increased theta and gamma power with decreased alpha, a profile that has been interpreted as a signature of effective encoding. Here, we tested whether SMEs reflect individual differences in mnemonic ability by analyzing over 1.3 million encoding events from a large free recall dataset. At the group level, alpha suppression and theta enhancement predicted successful encoding, while gamma did not predict subsequent memory after controlling for serial position. citation_details.title: Brain Networks and Non-invasive Brain Stimulation in Alzheimer’s Disease: From Mechanistic Insights to Clinical Applications
citation_details.author: Jie Ma, Juanjuan Lu, Qi-Hao Guo, Xu‐Yun Hua, Jian‐Guang Xu
citation_details.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a continuously progressing clinical and biological spectrum, in which synaptic dysfunction and the resulting brain network abnormalities serve as core mechanisms underlying the transition from subjective cognitive decline (SCD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to dementia. This chapter is organized into three sections. The first section provides an overview of brain network alterations across the different stages of AD, including both resting-state and task-related networks. The second section introduces methods for assessing brain network function, such as multimodal neuroimaging and EEG. The third section focuses on non-invasive brain stimulation techniques for AD, including transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), which aim to restore cognitive function by modulating brain network activity.

citation_details.title: Specialized recall procedures
citation_details.author: Michael J. Kahana, Sean Matthew Polyn, Lynn J. Lohnas
citation_details.abstract: Studies of memory search using the free recall paradigm have advanced our understanding of human memory for more than a century. Here, we review seven specialized recall procedures that depart from methodological orthodoxy: the inter-list repetition procedure, the list-before-last procedure, the recall-by-category procedure, the final-free recall procedure, the overt-rehearsal procedure, the externalized recall procedure, and the spatial-temporal recall procedure. Key empirical findings from each of these procedures have challenged existing theories and led to theoretical advances.

citation_details.title: What masking geometry works best for EEG foundation models?
citation_details.author: Pierre Guetschel, Bruno Aristimunha, Yassine El Ouahidi, Arnaud Delorme A, Thomas Moreau, Michael Tangermann
citation_details.abstract: EEG foundation models hold promise for scalable brain-signal decoding across clinical and cognitive neuroscience applications, yet their pre-training pipelines remain poorly understood. Among design choices, the masking strategy is particularly critical: it determines what the network must predict and from which context. Yet it has never been ablated in isolation, as each new model bundles a new masking strategy with a new backbone and objective. In this paper, we formalize the design choices for spatio-temporal masking strategies and train various models with a single pipeline under varying masking configurations across two SSL frameworks (MAE and JEPA). We then systematically evaluate the resulting 58 pre-trained models on the 12 datasets of OpenEEGBench under a linear probe. Both frameworks agree on an optimal masking configuration and on shared failure modes. Outside these, performance is robust: 11 MAE and 9 JEPA configurations are statistically indistinguishable from the best. We further identify a novel JEPA-specific failure mode, tagged bias-inflation collapse, invisible to standard detectors. With a well-chosen mask, our pipeline reaches REVE-level downstream performance at a fraction of REVE's pre-training compute.

citation_details.title: EEGDash Corpus: A Training-Ready Public Corpus for EEG Foundation Models
citation_details.author: Kuber Shahi, Bruno Aristimunha, Arnaud Delorme A
citation_details.abstract: Foundation models for electroencephalography (EEG) are pretrained on tens of thousands of hours of recordings, and their accuracy grows with that amount. Such data is hard to assemble. The largest sources are clinical archives that cannot be redistributed, and the public sources are spread over several archives, file formats, and licences. We release eegdash-corpus-v0, a training-ready corpus of 77 public EEG datasets, as the gated Hugging Face dataset EEGDash/eegdash-corpus-v0 with the SHA-256 of every file. REVE, the largest published EEG foundation model, names 89 datasets as its pretraining corpus. Twelve cannot be redistributed: four clinical archives that hold 82% of its hours, and eight under no-derivatives licences. The corpus holds the 76 others that REVE's sampling rate allows and one more from REVE's release card: 77 datasets, 14,075 hours from 7,272 subjects, 5.0 million 10-second samples and 6.21 billion tokens per epoch. Every dataset is fetched through EEGDash, converted once with REVE's recipe, and stored in its own buckets of a chunked Zarr store with its licence recorded beside it, so a model can train on the whole store or on any subset of datasets. To test that the store pretrains a model, we retrain REVE-Base from scratch twice with the authors' code, changed only in how it reads data, and score it on seven public OpenEEGBench tasks. It reaches 0.331 under linear probing and 0.273 after fine-tuning, against 0.333 and 0.325 for the released model and 0.200 and 0.205 for an untrained encoder. The converter, the conversion reports, and the loader changes are released with the corpus.

citation_details.title: REVE: A Foundation Model for EEG - Adapting to Any Setup with Large-Scale Pretraining on 25,000 Subjects
citation_details.author: Yassine El Ouahidi, Jonathan Lys, Philipp Thölke, Nicolas Farrugia, Bastien Pasdeloup, Vincent Gripon, Karim Jerbi, Giulia Lioi
citation_details.abstract: Foundation models have transformed AI by reducing reliance on task-specific data through large-scale pretraining. While successful in language and vision, their adoption in EEG has lagged due to the heterogeneity of public datasets, which are collected under varying protocols, devices, and electrode configurations. Existing EEG foundation models struggle to generalize across these variations, often restricting pretraining to a single setup, resulting in suboptimal performance, in particular under linear probing. We present REVE (Representation for EEG with Versatile Embeddings), a pretrained model explicitly designed to generalize across diverse EEG signals. REVE introduces a novel 4D positional encoding scheme that enables it to process signals of arbitrary length and electrode arrangement. Using a masked autoencoding objective, we pretrain REVE on over 60,000 hours of EEG data from 92 datasets spanning 25,000 subjects, representing the largest EEG pretraining effort to date. REVE achieves state-of-the-art results on 10 downstream EEG tasks, including motor imagery classification, seizure detection, sleep staging, cognitive load estimation, and emotion recognition. With little to no fine-tuning, it demonstrates strong generalization, and nuanced spatio-temporal modeling. We release code, pretrained weights, and tutorials to support standardized EEG research and accelerate progress in clinical neuroscience.
